strengths: Elegant and physically motivated core idea: DUS reduces the joint entropy gap of parallel unmasking by forcing spatial separation (dilation) between simultaneously revealed tokens, preventing the typical clustering behavior of confidence-based planners.
Training-free and model-agnostic: The method is purely inference-only and requires zero modifications or retraining of the underlying MDLM.

Comprehensive empirical validation: Evaluated across 5 models (LLaDA, Dream, DiffuCoder) and 7 benchmarks (math, code, general knowledge, instruction following), showing significant Pareto improvements (speed vs. accuracy) over established baselines.
Strong theoretical backing: Provides analytical guarantees bounding the parallel-sampling surrogate's approximation of the joint entropy under fast-mixing assumptions.
Highly practical hybrid extension: Showing that the dilation principle can be successfully used as a drop-in post-filter for adaptive samplers (EB/CB) to improve their performance.
weaknesses: Degradation under very large block sizes: While DUS significantly outperforms confidence-based baselines under larger block sizes, there is still a noticeable drop in accuracy in the single-block limit ($B=G$), indicating a fundamental bottleneck of parallel decoding in long sequences.

Reliance on the fast-mixing assumption for the theoretical proofs: The theoretical bounds rely on a stationary, ergodic variable-length Markov chain (VLMC) assumption. Though the empirical results show robust performance on code and math where this assumption is violated, the theoretical guarantee itself is constrained to this idealized setting.
Sensitivity of hyperparameters: The optimal skip threshold $c$ and base $a$ can be somewhat task-dependent, necessitating some empirical search to maximize performance on a new dataset.

strengths: Well-motivated theoretical foundation: Casting parallel unmasking as an optimization of the entropy gap between parallel independent sampling and joint sampling is elegant. Under the assumption of a fast-mixing VLMC, the authors provide mathematical guarantees showing that spatial dilation minimizes this gap.

Strong empirical performance: The proposed Dilated Unmasking Scheduler (DUS) is evaluated extensively across 5 distinct model variants and diverse benchmarks (including GSM8K, MATH500, HumanEval, MBPP, BBH, MMLU-Pro, and IFEval). It consistently and significantly outperforms the standard confidence-based parallel planners at equivalent latency budgets.

Simplicity and model-agnostic nature: DUS is a plug-and-play, inference-only strategy that requires no retraining, architectural changes, or auxiliary guidance models. Its computational overhead is negligible compared to the denoiser forward pass.

Innovative hybrid extension: Showing that the dilated-spacing principle can be applied as a drop-in post-filter to improve existing adaptive samplers (like EB and CB) demonstrates the versatility and broad applicability of the core concept.
weaknesses: Real-world language data often violates the fast-mixing assumption, especially in structured settings like code or step-by-step mathematical reasoning. Although the authors acknowledge this limitation and show strong empirical robustness, the theoretical proofs rely heavily on this assumption.

Sensitivity to block-size configuration: The performance of DUS is closely tied to the chosen block size B. While moderate block sizes (B=16, 32) perform well, extreme block sizes can either limit parallelism (small B) or degrade context quality and cause error propagation (large B).

Performance degradation at high speedups: Although DUS maintains much better accuracy than confidence-based baselines, there is still a noticeable accuracy gap between high-speedup configurations (such as B=64) and the slow, token-by-token baseline (x1 speedup).

strengths: Highly intuitive and elegant core idea: spacing out simultaneously unmasked tokens to minimize conditional dependence, thereby closing the joint-to-marginal entropy gap of parallel sampling.
Practical and inference-only: Requires zero retraining, model architectural changes, or auxiliary guide models, making it a drop-in scheduler for discrete diffusion language models.
Thorough theoretical framing: Soundly connects token spacing to conditional mutual information decay using a fast-mixing variable-length Markov chain (VLMC) model.

Extensive empirical evaluation: Validated across multiple model families (LLaDA, Dream, DiffuCoder) and diverse tasks spanning math, reasoning, coding, and instruction following, demonstrating consistent improvements over confidence-based parallel planners.
High-quality qualitative analysis: Color-coded decoding paths in the appendix clearly show how DUS prevents spatial clustering and repetitive degeneration compared to baseline decoders.
Generalizability: The dilated spacing principle is successfully extended to improve standard adaptive samplers (EB/CB) as a post-filter.
weaknesses: The theoretical guarantees rely on a stationary, ergodic VLMC with fast-mixing properties, which does not fully capture the long-range dependencies and global constraints inherent in realistic programming languages or structured text.

While DUS significantly outperforms confidence-based parallel planners, there remains a performance gap between highly accelerated MDLMs (e.g., larger block sizes $B \ge 32$) and fully autoregressive baselines on complex reasoning tasks.

The method is evaluated primarily within the semi-autoregressive block-wise setting; scaling to fully non-autoregressive generation (i.e., $B=G$) causes a significant drop in accuracy, although it still remains superior to baseline schedulers.

strengths: The paper addresses a highly relevant bottleneck in discrete masked diffusion language models (MDLMs): the high inference latency of token-by-token or poorly planned parallel generation.

The proposed Dilated Unmasking Scheduler (DUS) is training-free and model-agnostic, making it easy to plug into existing pre-trained and instruction-tuned MDLMs without retraining or auxiliary models.

Strong theoretical motivation showing that DUS minimizes the mutual information between concurrently unmasked tokens (maximizing spatial separation), thereby approximating the joint entropy bound under a fast-mixing Markov assumption.

Comprehensive experimental evaluation across multiple state-of-the-art MDLMs (LLaDA, Dream, DiffuCoder) and diverse tasks (math, code, general knowledge), consistently outperforming traditional confidence-based planners, especially at high speedup rates (e.g., 6.4x and 10.7x).
Thoughtful ablation studies demonstrating why the dilated-incremental scheduling is superior to fixed-k parallel unmasking schedules.
weaknesses: The theoretical guarantees rely on a first-order Markov assumption for language. Modern transformer-based language models exhibit long-range dependencies, so this assumption is physically unrealistic, and the paper would benefit from discussing how this gap affects the theoretical bounds in practice.

The 'Skip Mechanism' (Section 3.6, Point 3) is introduced as an optional feature, but its implementation details, threshold selection, and empirical impact are not clearly evaluated or detailed in the main experiments.

Clarity around block-wise dependencies could be improved: it is not entirely clear how context from previously decoded blocks affects the DUS schedule of the current block, or if the dilation pattern is reset entirely at block boundaries.

strengths: Highly practical, training-free, and model-agnostic approach that directly plugs into any standard MDLM (like LLaDA, Dream, or DiffuCoder) without requiring any architecture modifications or retraining.

Strong and intuitive theoretical grounding. By framing parallel unmasking as entropy minimization over a fast-mixing Markov chain, the authors elegantly demonstrate why traditional confidence-based unmasking suffers from redundancy (high mutual information between adjacent/correlated tokens) and why dilated spacing is theoretically optimal.

Extensive and convincing empirical results. DUS is evaluated across multiple domains (math, code, general knowledge) using several 7B-8B parameter state-of-the-art MDLMs, showing consistently large accuracy gains (up to 20-40% relative improvement) at high speedup factors compared to the confidence-based baseline.

Insightful ablation studies (e.g., Table 3) that successfully isolate the benefit of the dilated-incremental schedule, revealing that even a random planner benefits significantly when forced to space out its unmasked tokens.
weaknesses: The theoretical analysis assumes a first-order Markov chain with fast-mixing properties. While mathematically convenient and standard for such proofs, natural language exhibits complex, long-range dependencies that violate this assumption, meaning the theory only partially explains the empirical success.

The baseline comparisons are somewhat narrow. While the standard self-confidence planner is the most natural baseline, the evaluation would be much stronger if it compared against other recent scheduling/planning methods mentioned in the related work, such as EB-Sampler or Jump Your Steps.

The 'Skip Mechanism' introduced at the end of Section 3.6 is not thoroughly evaluated or ablated. It is unclear how much of the performance gain is due to the deterministic dilated schedule versus this adaptive skip mechanism, and the paper lacks clear guidelines on how its threshold parameter is tuned.

Minor clarity issues in Section 3.5: the description of merging $P_R$ into $P_{R-1}$ when $|P_R| < |P_{R-1}|$ is slightly hand-wavy and could be detailed more formally to ensure perfect reproducibility.

strengths: The proposed Dilated Unmasking Scheduler (DUS) is a simple, elegant, and training-free method that significantly improves the speed-accuracy trade-off of masked diffusion language models (MDLMs).
Solid theoretical support using a first-order Markov chain assumption and maximal correlation coefficient bounds to prove that DUS minimizes joint conditional entropy.
Comprehensive and rigorous evaluation across multiple state-of-the-art MDLMs (LLaDA, Dream, DiffuCoder) and diverse challenging tasks (mathematical reasoning, code generation, and multi-choice QA).
Impressive empirical improvements (e.g., recovering up to 27% absolute accuracy on GSM8K under large speedup settings compared to standard confidence-based planners).
weaknesses: The theoretical framework relies on a first-order Markov assumption. While this is standard for tractability, a discussion on how long-range dependencies in natural language affect the bounds would strengthen the paper.

The 'Skip Mechanism' mentioned in Section 3.6 is an interesting hybrid feature, but its implementation details, parameters (e.g., thresholds), and exact ablation are not fully explored or clarified in the main text.

In Table 3, the combination of self-confidence selection with incremental scheduling ('Conf. inc.') results in a severe performance drop. While the paper explains why random benefits from incremental spacing, a deeper intuitive explanation of this confidence-based failure mode would be valuable.
